terms.latin: nimis coctus, nimis cocta, nimis coctum
terms.comment: A description of ours: we have found no Latin word for overcooked in Lewis & Short, Traupman, Morgan–Owens, or Levi–Bini, nor a set phrase in Cato, Columella, or Apicius. Columella’s warning not to let grapes cook through (nē excoquantur) comes nearest; see the next term.

terms.gloss: boil away; cook right through, cook too long
evidence: Col. 12.16.1: nec rūrsus committere, ut excoquantur
Cato Agr. 107: ūsque coquitō, dum dīmidium excoquās
terms.comment: To boil out or boil away (Cato boils a liquid down by half), and so to cook a thing right through: Columella dips grapes in boiling lye only until they change colour, and not so long that they cook through.

phrases.latin: dum dēcolōrentur, nec rūrsus committere, ut excoquantur; nam quādam moderātiōne temperāmentōque opus est
phrases.english: until they change colour, but not to let them cook through either: it takes a sense of measure and balance

phrases.latin: Nimis diū coxistī holera; jam nimis mollia sunt.
phrases.english: You’ve cooked the vegetables too long; now they’re too soft.

sources: Lewis & Short: excoquo · Lewis & Short: coquo
